input: In this worked example, we consider a flat wall made of stainless steel, with a thickness of 20 mm, which separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference that has been measured across the wall is 97 K. Under conditions of steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through the wall can be calculated by dividing the product of the thermal conductivity and the temperature difference by the thickness of the wall. Expressing the thickness in metres as 0.02 m and carrying out this calculation gives a heat flux of 77600 W m-2. It is important to note that this estimate relates solely to conduction through the wall itself. Surface (film) resistances have been excluded from this estimate, and it should be understood that including them would have the effect of lowering the flux, since the films would introduce additional resistances in series with the resistance of the wall. Consequently, the value that has been obtained here should be regarded as an idealised figure based on the properties of the wall alone, and the flux that would be observed in practice, taking the surface films into account, would be somewhat lower than the figure calculated above. In addition, it should be appreciated that the calculation treats the wall as a homogeneous slab of material with a single, uniform thermal conductivity, and it takes no account of any variation in the properties of the material with temperature, nor of any imperfections in the contact between the wall and the streams on either side of it. The approach that has been followed here is deliberately simple in nature, and its purpose is to provide a clear estimate of the conductive flux through the wall under the stated conditions, on the basis of the properties and measurements that have been provided.
target:
A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 97 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall gives the heat flux as the conductivity times the temperature difference, divided by the thickness. With the thickness expressed as 0.02 m, the flux is 77600 W m-2. The flux is heat per unit wall area, so the result carries no wall area with it: the total rate through any given wall follows from this figure multiplied by that wall's area. The estimate is for conduction through the metal alone. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux, because the films add resistance in series with the wall and take part of the overall temperature difference that the two streams present. The stated flux is therefore the wall-only value at the measured difference across the wall itself, and it is an upper value for the flux the two streams would actually exchange through the wall and its films together.

One-dimensional conduction is the right model where the wall is flat and its area is large against its thickness, so that edge losses carry a negligible share of the heat and the temperature varies only through the thickness. Steady state means the temperature difference is read after the wall has settled. While conditions are changing, the wall stores or releases heat, and the flux entering one face differs from the flux leaving the other; the stated figure applies once that storage has ended. The dependence the result rests on is direct: the flux rises in proportion to the conductivity and to the temperature difference, and falls in inverse proportion to the thickness, so a wall twice as thick passes half the flux at the same measured difference. The result is a single number on a stated basis: conductivity and temperature difference measured on the wall, thickness as built, films excluded.
